rows.grounds: compound denoting path starting from Sadāśiva

items.question: Why does the path beginning with Sadāśiva require an eternal material cause?
premises: The path beginning with Sadāśiva is subject to change.
Changeable entities require a material cause.
Such a material cause must be eternal.
items.inference: Therefore the path beginning with Sadāśiva presupposes an eternal material cause.
items.plain_english: This path beginning with Sadāśiva is also subject to change; therefore it must have an eternal material cause.

items.question: How can an earthen pot ultimately have Māyā as its material cause?
premises: A pot is made of earth.
An earthen pot can still be traced to a deeper material cause.
That deeper material cause is Māyā.
items.inference: Therefore even an earthen pot has Māyā as its material cause.
items.plain_english: Even a pot made of earth may have Māyā as its material cause.

items.question: What is the ultimate material cause of a pot whose immediate material is clay?
premises: Clay is the direct material cause of a pot.
A direct material cause can itself have a prior cause.
Māyā is that prior material cause.
items.inference: Therefore Māyā alone is the ultimate material cause of the pot.
items.plain_english: Even when clay is the direct material of a pot, Māyā alone is its material cause indirectly.

items.question: What common material nature belongs to every produced entity such as kalā?
premises: Whatever thing arises is a produced entity.
Kalā is an example of such a produced entity.
All produced entities are constituted of Māyā.
items.inference: Therefore every arisen thing, like kalā, is Māyā.
items.plain_english: Whatever thing arises is this Māyā, just as kalā is.

items.question: By what authoritative means is the Māyā-nature of produced things established?
premises: The claim about produced things has been stated.
Trustworthy testimony can establish such claims.
This claim is supported by trustworthy testimony.
items.inference: Therefore this point is established by authoritative statement.
items.plain_english: This is also established by trustworthy testimony; such is the meaning.

items.question: What constitutes transformation in things according to this definition?
premises: Things can exist in successive states.
Transformation involves leaving a prior state.
The prior state is abandoned in the process.
items.inference: Therefore transformation is the abandonment of a thing's previous state.
items.plain_english: Transformation of things is indeed the abandonment of their previous state.

items.question: How is the state of buttermilk understood in relation to curd?
premises: Curd can undergo transformation.
Buttermilk is a state arising from curd.
This resulting state is observed and ascertained.
items.inference: Therefore the buttermilk state is ascertained as a transformation of curd.
items.plain_english: And in the case of curd, like buttermilk, the state of buttermilk is ascertained there.

items.question: What remains identical through the successive states of milk and curd?
premises: Milk and curd are successive states.
An existing entity persists through these states.
The same one thing appears first as milk and then as curd.
items.inference: Therefore one existing thing persists through the states of milk and curd.
items.plain_english: Indeed one existing thing is first milk and then curd.

items.question: How has the preceding account of transformation been presented?
premises: The topic of transformation has been discussed.
The discussion was not merely brief.
It was presented in detail.
items.inference: Therefore the account has been shown in detail.
items.plain_english: This has been shown in detail.

items.question: What kind of material cause underlies the tattvas and their derivative states?
premises: The tattvas and tāttvika states are produced realities.
Produced realities require a material cause.
Their material cause must be imperishable.
items.inference: Therefore the material cause of tattvas and tāttvika states is imperishable.
items.plain_english: The material cause of the tattvas and tāttvika states is imperishable.

rows.grounds: present middle participle or verb form in context

items.question: Why is Māyā's transformation not a defect in its imperishable nature?
premises: Māyā is the imperishable material cause.
Transformation can occur in only a part of a whole.
The ghee-worm analogy illustrates partial transformation.
items.inference: Therefore Māyā transforms by one part alone and there is no fault.
uncertainties: pariṇamata taken as finite verb in context
items.plain_english: By the analogy of the ghee-worm, Māyā transforms by one part alone; thus there is no fault.

rows.grounds: negated candidate cause; aṇu as individual self

items.question: Which entities are excluded as material causes of the pure path?
premises: The pure path requires a specific account of causation.
Māyā, the Lord, the individual self, and power are considered as candidates.
None of these serve as the material cause of the pure path.
items.inference: Therefore Māyā, the Lord, the individual self, and power are not the material cause of the pure path.
items.plain_english: Neither Māyā, nor the Lord, nor the individual self, nor power is the material cause of the pure path.

rows.grounds: past passive participle, sandhi before nantatejasā

items.question: By whose infinite energy is Māyā agitated to produce those entities?
premises: Māyā is involved in the production of those entities.
Māyā requires agitation to function as material cause.
This agitation is effected by infinite energy.
items.inference: Therefore Māyā is agitated by one possessing infinite energy.
items.plain_english: For that Māyā of them is agitated by one of infinite energy.

items.question: Who is identified as the agent possessing the infinite energy that agitates Māyā?
premises: Māyā is agitated by infinite energy.
Such agency belongs to a lordly being.
That being is identified as the Lord.
items.inference: Therefore the agent is the Lord.
items.plain_english: Thus, it is the Lord.

items.question: What characteristics place certain realities within the impure Māyā path?
premises: Some realities are impure and inert.
Such realities belong to the path of Māyā.
These characteristics distinguish them from the pure path.
items.inference: Therefore impurity, inertness, and belonging to the Māyā path characterize these realities.
items.plain_english: Because of being impure and inert, and likewise because of belonging to the path of Māyā.

rows.grounds: ablative of reason; aṇu as individual self

items.question: Why are transformation and related processes associated with objects of bound selves?
premises: Certain realities are experienced by bound individual selves.
Objects of such experience undergo transformation and arising.
These processes mark their conditioned nature.
items.inference: Therefore transformation and arising belong to what is experienced by bound selves.
items.plain_english: Because they are to be experienced by bound individual selves, and also because of transformations and the like.

items.question: What accompanies the production of kalā and the other principles?
premises: Kalā and other principles are produced.
Their production involves embodied conditions.
Bodies and related factors are included in that production.
items.inference: Therefore the production of kalā and others is accompanied by body and related factors.
items.plain_english: In the production of kalā and the others, it is endowed with body and so forth.

items.question: What analogy illustrates the agent's role in shaping material into a product?
premises: A material can be shaped into a product.
A blacksmith shapes gold into a crown.
This illustrates an agent acting on material.
items.inference: Therefore the blacksmith shaping gold into a crown serves as the analogy.
items.plain_english: Like a blacksmith with gold in the act of producing a crown.

rows.grounds: present passive verb, sandhi before nantanāthena

items.question: How does Lord Ananta's agitation of Māyā resemble a potter working with clay?
premises: Māyā is agitated by Lord Ananta.
Clay is agitated by a potter.
Both cases involve an agent acting on a material cause.
items.inference: Therefore Lord Ananta agitates Māyā as a potter agitates clay.
items.plain_english: It is agitated by Lord Ananta, as clay is by a potter.

items.question: Within what cognitive domain is agency observed in embodied beings?
premises: Embodied beings exhibit agency.
Agency is observed in relation to conceptual knowledge.
This observation is restricted to objects of conceptual knowledge.
items.inference: Therefore the agency of embodied beings is seen only in the domain of conceptual knowledge.
items.plain_english: The agency of embodied beings is seen only with regard to objects of conceptual knowledge; such is the meaning.

items.question: Into how many divisions is speech classified beginning with vaikharī?
premises: Sound is identified with speech in this context.
Speech is analyzed by division.
The division beginning with vaikharī is fourfold.
items.inference: Therefore that sound, as speech, is fourfold by division beginning with vaikharī.
items.plain_english: But that sound, as speech, is fourfold by division, beginning with vaikharī and so on.

items.question: What establishes bindu in relation to sound as its material cause?
premises: Sound requires a material cause.
Bindu is proposed as that material cause.
This role establishes bindu in that context.
items.inference: Therefore bindu is established as the material cause of sound.
items.plain_english: There, by being the material cause of sound, bindu is also established.

items.question: Who is regarded as the knowledge-bodied agitator in this account?
premises: An agitator is required in the process described.
This agitator is characterized as knowledge-bodied.
Lord Ananta is identified with this role.
items.inference: Therefore Lord Ananta is regarded as the knowledge-bodied agitator.
items.plain_english: Lord Ananta, whose body is knowledge, is regarded as the agitator.

items.question: Why is this great lord not considered the material cause constituted by Māyā?
premises: Lord Ananta has been identified as the agitator.
An agitator is distinct from the material cause.
Māyā functions as the material cause in this context.
items.inference: Therefore this great lord is not the material cause that is Māyā.
items.plain_english: Therefore this great lord is likewise not the material cause that is Māyā.
